does-a-bid-due-today-count-as-a-day-rema.text:
← Contractor Bid Readiness Checklist

Does a bid due today count as a day remaining?

No — it reads as zero. The table below is the exact fixture the checklist's own test suite runs to confirm the day count, and the urgency label it drives, match what the calendar actually says.

What the checklist reports, checked at a fixed moment

All rows checked from 2099-01-01 09:00 or 23:30 local time, both giving the same day count — the count depends only on the calendar date, never the time of day.
Due dateDays remainingWording shownUrgency
2099-01-01 (today)0The deadline is today.urgent
2099-01-02 (tomorrow)11 day remains.urgent
2099-01-08 (in a week)77 days remain.normal
2098-12-31 (passed yesterday)−1The deadline passed 1 day ago.past-due

Urgency turns to urgent at 2 days remaining or fewer, including zero, and to past-due the moment the count goes negative — there is no window where a bid that can no longer be filed is still labeled urgent.

Both the deadline and the moment you check are set to local midnight before the subtraction, so the count is whole calendar days, never a fraction of one. That also means the same due date returns the same day count whether you check first thing in the morning or right before the browser tab closes at night, and it holds across a daylight-saving change, where the day itself is 23 or 25 hours long.

Open the checklist and add your own deadline to see the count and the urgency label together. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

This page explains arithmetic, not contracting or legal advice. It does not replace reading the original solicitation for its actual submission deadline and time zone.

Common questions

Does a bid due today count as a day remaining, or zero?

Zero. The checklist sets both the deadline and the current moment to local midnight before subtracting, so a bid due today reads as 0 days remaining no matter what time it is checked — 9am or 11:30pm the same day both read 0. An earlier version measured to the due date's last second and rounded up, which read a bid due today as 1 day remaining and one due tomorrow as 2, understating how little time was actually left.

Why does a deadline that passed overnight show past-due immediately instead of after a full day?

Because the day count is whole calendar days from local midnight, not hours since the deadline. A bid due 2099-01-01 checked the next morning already reads −1 day and past-due, whether it is 9am or 11:45pm that next day. The earlier per-second version produced a fraction between −1 and 0 for the first 24 hours after a deadline, which rounds up to 0 — so the page still called the bid urgent, not past-due, on the one day it could no longer be filed.

Does the count ever shift because of daylight saving time?

No. Both the deadline and today are collapsed to local midnight before the difference is taken, so a 23- or 25-hour day across a spring-forward or fall-back change cannot shift the day count by one.

Common questions

What does marking a requirement “Ready” versus “Attention” versus “Blocked” actually change?

Only items marked Ready count toward being done — anything left as Attention or Blocked shows up in the missing count and in the readiness report. Blocked exists as its own status, separate from Attention, so an item you cannot move forward without someone else (a subcontractor's certificate, a bond your surety hasn't issued yet) is visibly different from one that is simply not started.

How is the days-remaining count worked out, and why does it matter that today counts as zero?

Both the deadline and today are set to local midnight before the difference is taken, so a bid due today reads as 0 days remaining, not 1 — and a deadline that passed overnight reads as past-due within the same day rather than showing a confusing fractional number. Urgency turns to “urgent” at 2 days or fewer remaining and to “past-due” the moment the count goes negative, so the deadline pressure on the page matches what the calendar actually says. See does a bid due today count as a day remaining? for the worked table.

Does “all items ready” mean the bid is compliant or guaranteed to be accepted?

No. It means every requirement you listed is marked ready in your own tracking — it is only as complete as the list you built. This tool does not read the solicitation, does not check your documents for correctness, and cannot confirm the issuing authority will accept the submission. Always re-check the original RFP for a requirement you may not have listed.

Does this tool read or upload my bid documents?

No. It never opens or accepts files — it only tracks requirement names, owners, statuses, and notes that you type in, entirely in your browser. The downloaded Markdown report is generated locally and saved straight to your device.

Can I use this for more than one bid at a time?

Each browser session tracks one opportunity at a time on this page. Download the Markdown report for a bid before starting the next one so you keep a record, since the requirement list is not saved between opportunities automatically.

Can I share this checklist with a subcontractor or co-bidder?

Yes. "Copy shareable link" encodes the opportunity name, due date, and every requirement row — name, owner, status, note — into the link itself, after the "#". That part of a URL is never sent to a server or logged anywhere, so opening the link loads the same checklist without anything having been uploaded. It replaces retyping the list from a PDF or the downloaded Markdown report, and it is a snapshot: editing your copy after sending the link does not update anyone else's.

Is my checklist data uploaded anywhere?

No account and no network requests — everything stays in your browser. Anonymous feature counts are local-only, optional, and the checkbox above turns them off; Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control disable them automatically.

Checking a pasted public tender for deadline, bond, and insurance phrases instead of listing requirements by hand? The tender bid readiness checker scans solicitation text for those signals — nothing uploaded.

Free to use. Review the original solicitation and confirm requirements with the issuing authority. The checklist is an evidence aid, not a compliance or award determination.

vs-a-sticky-note-checklist.html.text:
← Contractor Bid Readiness Checklist

This checklist vs. a sticky note

A sticky note has one way to mark progress: crossed off or not. It cannot tell you that the one item still standing is waiting on somebody else, with the clock running.

What a sticky note or mental checklist is

A handwritten list, a mental tally, or a few crossed-off lines in a notebook is the fastest way to track a bid's requirements: write down what the solicitation asks for, cross each one off as it gets done. It needs no setup and it is how most independent contractors have always tracked a short list.

Its one signal is how many lines are crossed off. It has no way to mark an item as stuck on someone else's paperwork instead of simply not started, and no way to flag that the deadline is close enough that a stuck item needs escalating today rather than glanced at tomorrow.

What this checklist is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You list each requirement the solicitation asks for, assign it an owner, and mark it Ready, Attention, or Blocked. Only Ready items count toward being done. Blocked is tracked separately from Attention, and the submission deadline is reported in whole calendar days, tipping into urgent at two days or fewer and past-due the moment it goes negative. You get a status board built to surface the one requirement most likely to sink the bid, not a percentage that treats every remaining line the same.

Where to answer each question.
What a sticky note doesWhat this checklist does instead
Marks a line crossed off or not — one signal for every requirement.Tracks Ready, Attention, and Blocked separately, so a stuck item stays visibly distinct.
Has no way to say an item is waiting on someone else rather than simply not started.Marks Blocked as its own status and names the owner responsible for each requirement.
Reports progress as a flat count or percentage crossed off.Reports whether the bid is actually ready, and names the specific item still missing.
Has no deadline logic — "how many days are left" is whatever you work out in your head.Counts whole calendar days to the deadline and flags urgent or past-due automatically.
Cannot be handed to a subcontractor or co-bidder without retyping it.Encodes the whole checklist into a shareable link, and exports a Markdown report.

The same bid, read two ways

Five requirements, two days from the deadline: a bid bond, a certificate of insurance, references, and a signed proposal form are all ready. The fifth — a subcontractor's MBE certification — is blocked, waiting on the subcontractor to renew it.

A sticky note's tally reads 4 of 5, or 80% — a number most people read as nearly finished. This checklist reports the bid as not ready, names the one blocked item and that it depends on the subcontractor, and marks the whole submission urgent with 2 days remaining. Both readings come from the same five lines. Only one of them tells you that the remaining item is not a five-minute task — it needs a phone call today, not a glance tomorrow.

Common questions

What does a sticky note or mental checklist miss that this one does not?

A distinction between an item nobody has started and an item that is stuck waiting on someone else. A sticky note has one way to mark progress -- crossed off or not -- so a requirement blocked on a subcontractor's renewal looks identical to one you simply have not gotten to yet. This checklist tracks Blocked as its own status, separate from Attention, so the item that depends on another person is visibly different from the one that is only waiting on you.

Why is "80% done" the most dangerous reading of a bid checklist?

Because a percentage-crossed-off tally treats every remaining item as the same size problem. On this checklist's own worked example -- five requirements, four marked ready and one blocked on a subcontractor's certification, two days from the deadline -- a sticky note reads as 80% done, which sounds nearly finished. This checklist reports ready: false, one blocked item, and urgency: urgent, because the one requirement left is not a five-minute task: it depends on a third party and, with two days remaining, needs escalating today, not glanced at tomorrow.

Doesn't crossing an item off a list also tell you it's ready?

Only if every item that is not crossed off gets the same follow-up, which is exactly what a flat tally cannot guarantee. This checklist separates Ready, Attention, and Blocked, and only Ready counts toward being done -- so a requirement stuck on someone else's paperwork stays visibly distinct from one you have simply not opened yet, instead of collapsing into the same uncrossed line.

How big is the risk in practice?

On this checklist's own worked example: five requirements, four ready, one -- a subcontractor's MBE certification -- blocked, two days before the deadline. A sticky note's tally reads 4 of 5, or 80%, which most people read as nearly finished. This checklist reports the bid as not ready, names the one blocked item and who it is waiting on, and marks the whole bid urgent, because a blocked item with two days left is the one requirement that can still sink the submission -- and it is the one a percentage tally hides best.

Does this checklist require me to stop using my own tracking method?

No. It is a free pass at one solicitation's requirements, not a replacement for however you already run your business. Some contractors will keep a sticky note for quick personal reminders and reach for this checklist specifically when a bid has several requirements, more than one owner, or a tight deadline -- the situations where a flat tally is most likely to hide a blocked item.

vs-jobtread.html.text:
← Contractor Bid Readiness Checklist

This checklist vs. JobTread

Two different jobs: JobTread is an account-based construction management platform for running a contractor's whole sales, estimating, and scheduling pipeline. This page is a free, private worksheet for one bid's missing artifacts before its submission deadline.

What each tool is for

JobTread is a construction management platform built for residential and remodeling contractors: a client-facing CRM, estimating and proposal tools, budgeting, scheduling, and job financials, run through an ongoing account you and your team sign into. JobTread's own pricing and current feature list are not reachable from this session to confirm, so no dollar figure or plan name for JobTread is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — an account-based construction management platform covering sales, estimating, and job operations — are stated.

This checklist does none of what JobTread does. It has no CRM, no estimating engine, no job schedule, and no connection to any account — it stores and uploads nothing. It takes the requirements one solicitation lists, lets you assign an owner and a status to each, tracks the submission deadline as whole days remaining, and produces a downloadable Markdown report. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
I need a CRM, estimating, budgeting, and scheduling run through one account for every job.JobTread, or a comparable platform — running the whole job pipeline is not something this checklist does.
What is still missing from this specific bid before the deadline?This checklist — free, instant, private, no account.
How many days are actually left to submit, and when does that tip into urgent or past-due?This checklist's readiness report, worked out to whole calendar days.
How do I turn a won bid into a scheduled, budgeted job with a client record?JobTread, or your own job-management platform — this checklist stops at submission, not award.
Can I hand a private, dated readiness record to a partner or estimator before deciding to submit?This checklist's downloadable Markdown report, generated locally.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This checklist: no. JobTread is used through a JobTread account.

Most contractors get different value from each: JobTread (or a comparable platform) for running the sales-to-completion pipeline as an ongoing account, and a private checklist like this one for an instant, no-login pass at what a specific bid still needs before its deadline. This page's own figures are a readiness record, not a job schedule, a budget, or a CRM entry.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the checklist runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this checklist or JobTread?

Both, for different jobs, and a contractor who already runs client and job data through JobTread can still use this checklist for the narrow moment before a bid goes out the door. JobTread is a construction management platform built for residential and remodeling contractors: a client-facing CRM, estimating and proposal tools, budgeting, scheduling, and job financials, run as an ongoing account you and your team sign into. This checklist does none of that. It takes the requirements one solicitation lists — documents, forms, signatures, confirmations — and turns them into an owner-by-owner status board with a days-remaining count and a downloadable Markdown report, entirely in your browser, with no account and nothing uploaded. A contractor who wants estimating, scheduling, and job costing run through one system is better served by JobTread or a comparable platform; a contractor who wants an instant, private, no-login check of what is still missing before a specific bid's deadline is in the right place here.

Can JobTread track the bid-readiness items this checklist covers?

JobTread's proposal and job tools can carry a bid through its own workflow once you are set up in that account. This checklist is not a substitute for that workflow — it is a fast, account-free pass at one question: which requirements on this solicitation are ready, which need attention, and which are blocked, before the clock runs out. Some contractors will use this checklist once per unfamiliar solicitation and run everything else through JobTread or a similar platform; neither tool replaces the other.

Is this page affiliated with JobTread?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by JobTread, LLC. JobTread is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this checklist is and is not.
